paras: The lynching of Henry Pope took place at Summerville, Chattooga County, Georgia, on the night of April 30, 1888, when about fifty masked men took Pope, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him from the courthouse banisters. Pope had twice been convicted of assaulting a young white woman, but Governor Gordon had just respited him on evidence that he had been in Alabama that day. Wire briefs called him a "rapist," while an Atlanta dispatch printed in Wheeling and several Northern papers treated the case as the hanging of a probably innocent man.

According to the Savannah Morning News, Minnie Kendrick was assaulted by a Black man in woods near her home in Chattooga County on February 3, 1887. Pope was arrested in Cherokee County, Alabama, that May, and the Wheeling dispatch said Kendrick picked him from a group of twenty by "his wicked and cruel eyes." He was convicted at a special term on May 9, 1887, under armed guard against crowds.

Gordon respited Pope twice in 1887, Judge Maddox granted a new trial, and in March 1888 Pope was again convicted and sentenced to hang, on May 2 by the Morning News or May 8 by the Marietta Journal. Witnesses swore that he had been at work in Cherokee County, about fifty miles away, on the day of the assault; accounts counted five, eight or nine of them. After a petition from the judge and jury, Gordon granted a new sixty-day respite at the end of April.

Floyd County Sheriff J. C. Moore reached Summerville with orders to move Pope to Atlanta on a rainy night, but Judge Maddox and Sheriff Worsham advised waiting until sunrise. The Morning News said news of the respite, which Gordon had tried to keep secret, had arrived about two hours ahead of the sheriff.

About 2 o'clock, by Worsham's account, some fifteen armed men guarded his room in the jail while about fifty masked men demanded the keys and a rope bought in Rome. They led Pope about 150 yards to the courthouse and hanged him from the banisters at the top of the stairs, while armed men stood at the street corners. A doctor called by Judge Maddox found him dead. The Wheeling dispatch said instead that a "janitor" gave up the keys, and that Pope "declared his innocence to the last."

No report of an inquest, arrests or indictments appears in the coverage. The Wheeling dispatch said the deed was "greatly deplored all over the State." In July W. J. Allen applied for the governor's $500 reward, saying he had captured Pope in 1887 with John and Alex Garner, both Black.

The first Atlanta wire ran on May 1 and 2 in the Alexandria Gazette, the Memphis Appeal, the New-York Tribune and other papers. It said Pope had won several respites "by one pretext or another," under headlines from "Respited Too Often" and "Determined to Make Sure of Him" to "Another Outrage on Color." A second version, in the Emporia Weekly News and the Yorkville Enquirer, said "the people of the county lynched him."

The Savannah Morning News headlined its full account "Gov. Gordon's Third Respite Leads to Mob Law" and laid out the alibi without comment on the mob. The Marietta Journal wrote that "the respite enraged the people," and in July the Morning News still called Pope "the Chattooga county negro rapist."

In the North, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer ran the Atlanta dispatch under "Innocent Man Hanged," setting "the simple word of a sixteen-year old girl" against the testimony of "Alabama's best citizens." The Ohio Democrat and the Forrest City Times repeated the doubts about his guilt, and the Belmont Chronicle called it "the murder of Henry Pope" and an instance of "injustice to the negro in the South." In one digest, the Narragansett Herald called Pope "a colored murderer."

Accounts put the hanging at midnight Monday, about 2 o'clock, or, in the Wheeling dispatch dated May 2, "this morning, at half-past two." The charge appears as assault with attempt to commit rape in the Morning News but as rape in wire briefs, and the Belmont Chronicle placed the lynching in "Chattanooga, Ga."

bases: A mob of about fifty masked men took Pope from the Chattooga county jail and hanged him from the court-house banisters (A6, A10).

Pope, held under a respited death sentence, was seized from jail by about fifty masked armed men and hanged, and a doctor found him dead (A6, A10); the papers tie the act to his conviction for assaulting a white girl and anger at the governor's respite (A11, A13).
The Rome-dated Savannah account (A6), the Atlanta dispatch in Wheeling (A10), the Atlanta wires (A3, A13) and the Marietta Journal (A11) independently report the seizure and hanging.

accounts.label: Atlanta dispatch (Wheeling)
accounts.gist: Fifty masked men with shotguns forced the 'janitor' to give up the keys and hanged Pope, who was very likely innocent on the sworn evidence of nine Alabama men; the deed was deplored throughout the state.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Pope, a convicted 'negro' who had won several respites 'by one pretext or another', was taken from jail by a mob and hanged after a new respite.

accounts.gist: Pope was hanged at midnight from the court-house veranda; on news of the respite 'the people of the county lynched him.'

framing.detail: The Atlanta wire ran under headlines including 'Respited Too Often', 'Determined to Make Sure of Him', 'A Negro Hanged by a Mob' and 'Another Outrage on Color.'
The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Gov. Gordon's Third Respite Leads to Mob Law' and gave the alibi evidence and trial history without comment on the mob.
The Marietta Journal stated Pope was convicted 'for raping a white girl' and that the respite 'enraged the people'; the Morning News later still called him 'the Chattooga county negro rapist.'
The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer headlined 'Innocent Man Hanged. Masked Georgia Lynchers Commit a Gross Outrage on Justice.'
The Belmont Chronicle called it 'the murder of Henry Pope' and an instance of 'injustice to the negro in the South.'

versions.value: 'this morning, at half-past two' in a dispatch dated May 2

conflicts.note: The Wheeling dispatch also says 'Last night' and that Pope 'was to be hanged to-day', so its May 2 date is internally inconsistent; the Rome account with the officers' timeline (A6) is the most detailed.
The fullest and Georgia accounts written on the eve of the date (A4, A6) give May 2.
Accounts may count trial testimony and later affidavits differently.

versions.value: assault with attempt to commit rape

conflicts.note: The detailed accounts (A6, A10) describe an attempted assault; 'murderer' in a distant digest is unsupported.

versions.value: Sheriff Worsham, sleeping in the jail, under about fifteen shotguns

conflicts.note: A6 rests on the sheriff's own statement to Sheriff Moore.
The Belmont Chronicle's place name is an evident error; 'Somerville'/'Sommersville' are spelling variants (A17, A7).

Twice convicted of assault with attempt to commit rape upon Minnie Kendrick, under a respited death sentence; strong alibi evidence was reported.
Described as a mob of about fifty masked men; no organized band is named.
